analysis.one_liner: Bars giant digital ad companies from owning both sides of ad auctions and forces them to serve customers' interests.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 13, 2025 with 7 bipartisan cosponsors (5 Democrats, 2 Republicans), the bill has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite antitrust law for digital advertising, the system that decides which ads you see online and how much they cost. Companies earning more than $20 billion a year in digital ad revenue — chiefly Google — could no longer own the auction, the tool sellers use to offer ad space, and the tool buyers use to purchase it all at once, a setup that lets the middleman profit at both ends. Companies above $5 billion that broker ad deals would have to put their customers first, disclose their fees and routing practices, and protect user data. Violations could be enforced by the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that buy online ads — from national brands to local shops — would pay fewer hidden middleman fees and get better terms on each ad placement. Publishers, including news sites and content creators, would keep a larger share of the ad money that funds free online content. Web users gain privacy rules limiting how ad data is tracked and reused.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ad buyers, online publishers, and web users

how_it_helps.text: Companies with more than $20 billion in annual digital ad revenue may not own more than one type of ad marketplace service — for example, Google could not own both the ad exchange and the software that helps publishers sell their ad space.

Companies with more than $5 billion in digital ad revenue that broker ad deals must act in their customers' best interest, seek the best available terms for each order, and disclose bids, fees, and routing practices on request.
Brokerages must handle customer data with privacy safeguards, including anonymizing records before disclosure, and cannot require customers to waive class actions for claims under the bill.

Enforcement runs through the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and a private right of action with damages, plus an Antitrust Consumer Damages Fund to route recovered damages to people harmed.

analysis.who_pays: Large ad tech intermediaries — most directly Google, which the CRS summary names as the example — would have to divest part of their advertising business and absorb transparency, audit, and litigation costs. Some of that cost could pass through to ad prices while the market adjusts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Google and other large ad tech middlemen

drawbacks.text: Forced divestitures of ad tools many small businesses and publishers use every day could disrupt the ad market during a transition, and any court fight over a breakup would take years to resolve.

The benefits reach ordinary people indirectly — through lower ad costs for businesses and more revenue for publishers — rather than through a direct price cut or benefit, so gains may take years to show up.
Compliance and transparency duties for firms above $5 billion create real costs for the next tier of ad tech companies, not just the giants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is real but indirect: ad tech middlemen are estimated to keep a sizable share of every ad dollar, and the bill attacks the structural conflict of interest that lets them profit at both ends of their own auction. The cost is transition disruption and litigation risk for businesses that rely on these tools daily. On balance, a genuine pro-competition bill whose main downside is uncertainty during implementation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on March 13, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor action.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the AMERICA Act with original cosponsors Sens. Klobuchar (D), Schmitt (R), Warren (D), Welch (I), and Booker (D).
The bill was read twice in the Senate and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced.
Seven senators have cosponsored the bill: 5 of 45 Senate Democrats and 2 of 55 Senate Republicans.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large ad tech intermediaries the bill targets — above all Google — keep their current market position untouched, since no restriction has taken effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Google and the big ad middlemen

for.name: Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the AMERICA Act and led its introduction in the Senate.

for.name: Cosponsors (7 total)
for.role: 5 of 45 Senate Democrats and 2 of 55 Senate Republicans

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral — no action taken
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 13, 2025 and has taken no action on it since.

against.name: Google
against.what_they_did: The bill is drafted explicitly around Google's structure — the CRS summary names Google as the company that could not own both an ad exchange and publisher-selling software — and Google has publicly opposed similar ad tech antitrust legislation.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is split across the aisle: a Republican sponsor (Lee) with 5 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors, the same bipartisan pairing that carried earlier ad tech antitrust bills.

industries.industry: Digital ad tech intermediaries (Google, and firms above $20 billion)
industries.note: These firms currently own the auction, the seller tools, and the buyer tools, letting them take fees at both ends of the same ad trade. The bill would force divestiture and impose best-interest and disclosure duties; the CRS summary names Google as the direct example.
Ad buyers would face fewer hidden fees, a best-interest duty from their brokers, and a private right of action with damages for violations.
Publishers currently receive only a fraction of each ad dollar after middleman fees; breaking the stacked ownership should let them keep more of the ad money that funds online content.

industries.industry: Mid-tier ad tech firms ($5-20 billion revenue)
industries.note: They face new best-interest, transparency, and record-keeping duties above $5 billion in revenue, but could gain market share from any divestitures by the giants.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is nearly a year into the 119th Congress without a hearing or markup in the Judiciary Committee. Ad tech antitrust legislation has repeatedly stalled in committee despite bipartisan sponsorship, and with no scheduled action, the most likely path is that it remains pending until the Congress ends — unless a major court ruling against Google's ad business renews pressure to move it.
